query: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs phase stability and why, with relevance to retaining desirable combinations of high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness? Specify a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries of the hypothesis, supporting prior evidence, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In intermediate-Al-content Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, the formation of localized Al (and correlated Ni) clusters mediates a partial atomic ordering that kinetically retards deleterious phase transformations. This ordered clustering stabilizes a dual‐phase (or refined single phase) microstructure under simultaneous high-temperature oxidation, ion irradiation, and cryogenic deformation, thereby underpinning the alloy’s high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-cast or solution‐treated Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA with intermediate Al levels (e.g., Al mole fraction ~0.1–0.5) that initially exhibits a homogeneous FCC or FCC+BCC microstructure with a moderate degree of atomic randomness.
generation.intervention: Induce and control atomic clustering by applying a pre‐treatment (e.g., controlled compressive strain or a tailored heat treatment that promotes Al–Al clustering) and then subject the samples to sequential or simultaneous exposures of high‐temperature oxidation, ion irradiation, and cryogenic mechanical testing.
generation.conditions: High-temperature oxidation test around 900°C; ion irradiation using fluences similar to prior studies (e.g., ~1×10^16 cm⁻² with 3 MeV ions); and cryogenic tensile or compression testing at approximately 77 K. The experiments should include controlled variations in pre‐treatment to adjust the extent of clustering.
generation.structural_mediator: Localized Al–Al clustering (with correlated Ni association) that leads to partial ordering at the nanoscale, forming chemically distinct regions that impede long-range diffusion and phase coarsening.
generation.mechanism: The competition between high configurational entropy and the short-range attractive interactions (driving Al clustering) creates kinetically trapped ordered domains. These domains restrict atomic mobility and act as barriers to the diffusion-driven nucleation and growth of deleterious phases during high-temperature oxidation and under irradiation. Moreover, the resulting microstructural refinement and local chemical segregation enhance the formation of protective oxide scales and promote beneficial deformation mechanisms (e.g., twinning) at cryogenic temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline sample with more random atomic distribution, the clustered (ordered) sample will retain a finer and more stable microstructure with diminished precipitation (or formation of unwanted secondary phases) after high-temperature, irradiation, and cryogenic treatments. This will be evidenced by a more protective and uniform oxide scale in oxidation tests, reduced irradiation-induced precipitate growth, and superior low-temperature mechanical properties (e.g., higher yield strength and toughness).
generation.baseline: Identical HEA samples processed under standard conditions that do not promote enhanced Al clustering (e.g., using lower pre-strain or alternative heat treatments resulting in a more random atomic arrangement).
generation.boundary: This mechanism is proposed to dominate only in the intermediate Al-content regime (e.g., Al mole fraction ~0.1–0.5) where excessive phase separation (such as formation of σ phases at high Al contents) is not present. Its applicability under simultaneous multi-environment conditions (high temperature, irradiation, and cryogenic stress) is the focus of this study.
generation.uncertainty: This hypothesis builds on (1) MD simulation evidence of dominant Al–Al clustering and its ordering‐to‐clustering transitions under compressive loading (PMC4976365::web::012 and PMC4976365::web::005) and (2) irradiation studies showing that low atomic mobility (related to high configurational entropy) suppresses precipitation (PMC4999872::web::014). Extending these findings to explain the mechanistic link between atomic clustering and simultaneous phase stability under combined high-temperature oxidation, irradiation, and cryogenic conditions is new, and the quantitative interplay of these effects remains uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA samples with intermediate Al content. In one set, apply a pre-treatment (e.g., controlled compressive strain or specific heat treatment) to induce pronounced Al clustering; in the other set, use a processing route that minimizes atomic clustering. Subject both sets to a combined exposure regime that includes high-temperature oxidation (≈900°C), controlled ion irradiation (e.g., 3 MeV ions at ~1×10^16 cm⁻²), and cryogenic mechanical testing (≈77 K).
measurements: Atomic-scale microstructure analysis (via TEM and atom probe tomography) to quantify the degree of Al clustering and ordering.
Oxidation kinetics and oxide scale characterization (using XRD and EDS) to assess the formation and protective nature of the oxide layer.
Post-irradiation phase analysis (via TEM/EDS) for evidence of suppressed versus enhanced precipitation.
Cryogenic tensile testing to measure yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, ductility, and fracture toughness.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples with intentionally enhanced Al clustering do not show statistically significant improvement in retaining a stable, refined microstructure (evidenced by reduced formation of detrimental phases, improved oxide scale protection, lower radiation-induced precipitation, and superior cryogenic mechanical properties) compared to the baseline samples, then the hypothesis that localized Al clustering mediates the desired phase stability is falsified.
